content.text:
H1 doesn't explain the data on its own: the 15.27-day planet is clearly real, but the leftover scatter is about three times the limit and the residuals hold another strong signal near 10.4 days.

**Best fit: F1** (hypothesis H1, one planet, eccentricity free, period allowed to move ±10%)

| Quantity | Value | Judged against |
|---|---|---|
| Period | 15.269 d (started at 15.15 d) | — |
| Amplitude K | 40.09 m/s | 77 times the per-point noise (scaled by √N, the square root of the number of observations): a very strong detection |
| Eccentricity | 0.138 | — |
| Scatter (RMS) | 13.80 m/s | limit 4.37 m/s, **fails** |
| Reduced χ² | 24.8 | about 1 is expected for a good fit |
| BIC | 1690.8 | lower is better; 4894.5 below the no-planet model |
| Flags | none | the period isn't stuck on a search bound, and no wrong-start warning, so I didn't refit |

The fit uses 63 observations over a 37.3-day baseline.

**Peaks in what the fit leaves unexplained (residual periodogram)**
1. **10.40 d**, false-alarm probability 2.7×10⁻¹¹. This is a highly significant signal the fit doesn't account for. It isn't flagged as an alias or harmonic.
2. 6.39 d, false-alarm probability 0.0019. Also significant, so check it again once the 10.4-day signal is modelled.
3. All other peaks have false-alarm probabilities of 0.18 or higher, so they aren't significant.

The data contain a 15.27-day planet, but a one-planet model can't account for everything. Whether to test a two-planet hypothesis with periods of about 15.27 d and 10.40 d is the PI's call.
